title: Open Challenge: Efficient Approximation of Twin-Width for Unordered Graphs
statement_text: Efficiently approximating twin-width (that is, returning an $f(d)$-sequence when the twin-width of the input is at most $d$) remains an open challenge for unordered graphs.
context_text: A trigraph is a graph some of whose edges are red (the others black). Contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices $u,v$ of a trigraph merges them into a new vertex $w$, keeping $wx$ black if both $ux$ and $vx$ were black edges and making every other edge incident to $w$ red; the rest of the trigraph is unchanged. A contraction sequence of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is a sequence of trigraphs $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$ where $G_i$ has $i$ vertices and is obtained from $G_{i+1}$ by one contraction; it is a $d$-sequence if every $G_i$ has maximum red degree at most $d$, and the twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that $G$ admits a $d$-sequence. An approximation algorithm should, given a graph of twin-width at most $d$, output an $f(d)$-sequence for some function $f$; the authors specify later that it is unknown whether this can be done, say, in fixed-parameter time (parameterized by $d$). Many algorithmic results on bounded twin-width (e.g. fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking) assume that an $O(1)$-sequence is given with the input. Efficient approximation is known for totally ordered binary structures and for the known classes of bounded twin-width (bounded tree-width or rank-width, proper minor-closed classes, hereditary proper subclasses of permutation graphs, etc.), but remains open for general unordered graphs. The authors suggest one reason it may be delicate: $\Omega(\log n)$-subdivisions of $n$-vertex graphs have bounded twin-width while $o(\log n)$-subdivisions do not.
